Occurrences.Kwic: 水中擇乳須是鵝王
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T48/T48n2004.xml). Wansong’s Commentary and Chanting on Tiantong Jue’s Verse-Comments on the Ancients: Record of the Congrong Hermitage: Wansong Xingxiu says that selecting milk from water requires the goose king, using the image for the exacting work of distinguishing the participants’ handling of a case.

Senses.Explanation: To select the milk is to distinguish what matters within a mixture whose parts are not obvious at a glance. Zen masters make it the goose king’s capacity: unlike ducks, it selects milk from water, and the image becomes a verdict on whether someone can tell the live point of an encounter from its similar-looking alternatives. Wansong Xingxiu states the image most explicitly: selecting milk from water requires the goose king. He applies it to the fine discrimination needed to read how the participants handle a case. Guishan Lingyou calls Yangshan’s raised ear of grain “the goose king selecting milk” after Yangshan refuses a choice among green, yellow, and neither. The act distinguishes the point without accepting the offered alternatives. Dahui repeatedly uses the formula as a verdict. He applies it to Yangshan’s apparently contradictory statements about awakening, to two identical-looking offerings treated differently, and to the precise shortfall in Baofu’s answer. The goose-versus-duck contrast does not make the phrase a claim about birds or a general compliment for intelligence. In these records it names discrimination demonstrated in a concrete exchange, and Dahui adds that it requires seeing with one’s own eyes.

Senses.Explanation: A snake entering a straight bamboo tube must follow the tube’s narrow line even though the snake’s body naturally bends. The corpus explicitly contrasts command of teaching-language without command of the Chan encounter to a snake entering bamboo, and masters reuse the image to fault rigid, head-following-tail responses or a supposedly adaptive snake still trapped by its tube.
